opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it would get us a lot closer than people expect, but I don't think it's the endgame.

If you could run a few-hundred-billion-parameter model on 20 watts, you'd be in the same power envelope as the human brain. That would be a big milestone. But matching the wattage isn't the same as matching the efficiency. The brain isn't just doing inference on a static set of weights. It learns continuously, it's embodied, and it's doing a kind of probabilistic, generative modeling of the world all the time. Parameter count is a crude proxy for capacity. A synapse isn't a float32 weight. It's a noisy, stochastic, analog element doing something much richer per unit of energy.

The deeper point for me is how we get there. Right now we spend enormous amounts of energy fighting noise. Digital computing pushes transistors into deterministic regimes, pays the cost of erasing bits, shuttles data back and forth between memory and compute, and then uses pseudo-random number generators to simulate the stochasticity our algorithms actually want. That's fundamentally wasteful. Biology doesn't do that. It embraces the noise and uses thermal fluctuations as a computational resource.

So if you squeezed today's architectures down to 20 watts through better process nodes and clever engineering, you'd probably close part of the gap, maybe an order of magnitude or two on certain workloads. But the brain is still operating much nearer the thermodynamic limits of computation than anything we build. To truly match it, and then exceed it, you have to change the physics of the substrate. Probabilistic and generative AI needs to run natively on hardware that's itself stochastic, where sampling is what the physics does for free instead of something you simulate expensively.

That's why I think the 20-watt target is a useful North Star but a misleading finish line. The real goal isn't to just match the brain's energy budget. It's to build substrates that scale intelligence per joule far beyond biology. Biology is an existence proof, not an upper bound.

r001.rationale: The response says the model could close part of the gap by “an order of magnitude or two on certain workloads,” but it does not clearly estimate that it would be within roughly a factor of ten of the brain’s energy efficiency. It also distinguishes matching the brain’s wattage from matching its efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think that framing is a bit of a trap, because it assumes parameter count is the right unit of comparison, and I don't think it is. The brain has on the order of a hundred trillion synapses, so even a few hundred billion parameters is three orders of magnitude short on raw connectivity. But the deeper issue is that we're not really comparing like with like. Digital compute is doing a massive amount of work just moving bits around, shuttling weights between memory and the arithmetic units, maintaining perfect determinism, error-correcting every operation. The brain does none of that. It's a physical system computing in place. The synapse is both the memory and the compute, and it's operating right up against the thermal noise floor, basically using noise as a resource rather than fighting it.

So if you got a hundred-billion-parameter model running at 20 watts on conventional digital hardware, that would be an enormous engineering achievement, probably a few orders of magnitude better than where we are, but I'd argue it still wouldn't tell you much about brain-like efficiency. You'd have gotten there by squeezing the von Neumann paradigm as hard as it can go, not by actually changing the physics of how you compute.

The way I think about it is in terms of the thermodynamic cost per useful operation. Landauer gives you a floor, and the brain is maybe a few orders of magnitude above that floor. Our best GPUs are something like six or seven orders above it. That gap isn't going to close by shrinking transistors, because we're already running into the walls there. It closes by building hardware where the physics itself is doing the inference, where you let a noisy, analog, stochastic substrate relax into the answer rather than simulating that process with billions of exact floating point operations. That's the whole thesis behind thermodynamic computing, and it's why I'd say the 20-watt number matters less than the question of what kind of machine is drawing those 20 watts.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a 20-watt model would not tell us much about brain-like efficiency and gives no estimate that it would be within roughly a factor of ten; its stated comparison instead emphasizes substantial remaining gaps.

astra-6.text:
Well, it would be pretty remarkable, but the parameter count alone doesn’t tell you how close you are. You have to ask how much computation that model is doing, at what speed, and whether the 20 watts includes moving the weights around, memory, and everything else needed to run it.

The brain’s doing more than generating language. It’s processing sensory input, controlling a body, learning continuously—all within that power budget. So if you could run a model of that size at a useful speed on 20 watts, that would be a substantial achievement. But to say you’ve matched the brain’s energy efficiency, you’d want to compare the energy required for comparable tasks, with comparable capabilities. Otherwise, you’ve matched the power consumption without necessarily matching the efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
That would be pretty remarkable. If you could run a hundred- or few-hundred-billion-parameter model at a useful speed on 20 watts, you’d be in the same power range as the brain. But matching the power budget isn’t quite the same as matching its efficiency. You have to ask what computation you’re getting for those watts, and whether you’re counting memory, communication, and the rest of the system.

The brain is also continuously learning while it operates. So I’d call that a major milestone, but I wouldn’t infer brain-level energy efficiency from parameter count and power alone. You’d want to compare the capabilities, the throughput, and the ability to adapt.
